title: Why Ruth Handler Made Breast Forms in a Left and a Right
dek: After a mastectomy and her exit from Mattel, Ruth Handler started a small company in 1976 to make the breast form she could not buy.

story.event: Designing and selling the Nearly Me breast prosthesis after her own mastectomy
story.summary: After a mastectomy in 1970 and her departure from Mattel in 1975, Ruth Handler formed a company in 1976, Ruthton, to make Nearly Me, a silicone breast prosthesis sold in separate left and right versions and many sizes. She promoted it on talk shows and in department stores, fitted customers herself and hired women who had had mastectomies as fitters; sales passed $1 million by 1980, and she sold the company in 1991.
paragraphs: In 1970, while she was running Mattel, the toy company she and her husband had built and the maker of the Barbie doll she had created, Ruth Handler had breast cancer and a mastectomy that removed her left breast. Afterwards, a doctor suggested stuffing her bra with old nylon stockings. The alternatives on sale, cotton stuffing and padded bras, were in her words "designed by men, obviously."

Her life was coming apart in other ways too. In 1975, with the Securities and Exchange Commission investigating Mattel's reported earnings, she and her husband were forced out. In 1978 she was indicted for fraud and false reporting; she pleaded no contest, was fined $57,000 and was ordered to do 2,500 hours of community service.

What she still had was a manufacturer's eye and a problem she knew from her own body. In 1976 she formed a company, Ruthton, with a business partner. Working with a prosthetics specialist, she experimented with plastic and silicone until she had a form she called Nearly Me: liquid silicone in a polyurethane skin, with a firm foam back, in a wide range of sizes. Unusually, it came in separate left and right versions. "There has never been a shoemaker who made one shoe and forced you to put both your right and your left foot in it," she told The New York Times in 1977. Her aim, she said, was "that a woman could wear a regular brassiere and blouse, stick her chest out and be proud."

She promoted it in person. She toured department stores, invited late-night television hosts to touch her prosthesis, wrote invitations by hand to women with breast cancer, and fitted customers herself, hiring women who had also had mastectomies to do the same. She fitted the former first lady Betty Ford. By 1980 sales had passed $1 million, and in 1991 she sold the company.

quote.text: whoever conceals it makes it a reproach to himself; and therefore if you of your own accord are the first to acknowledge it, you cut the ground from under the feet of those who would sneer and politely insult you
quote.work: On the Firmness of the Wise Man (De Constantia Sapientis), in the Minor Dialogues
quote.locator: Dialogues, Book II, On the Firmness of the Wise Man, chapter XVII
quote.source_title: Minor Dialogues, Together With the Dialogue on Clemency, tr. Aubrey Stewart, Project Gutenberg eBook #64576
quote.connection: Seneca was writing about poverty, but his point fits Handler's talk-show rounds. Hiding a loss lets others decide what it means; naming it first takes that power away. Her openness was a kind of courage, and it was also how she reached her customers.

reflection: Handler did not need a survey to know the breast forms on offer were poor; she had worn them. Her own experience told her what was wrong, and her years in manufacturing told her how to make and sell something better. What she added was a refusal to treat the subject as unmentionable.

Some of what you know best may come from things you would rather not discuss: an illness, a failure, a long stretch of exhaustion. You do not owe anyone that story. But it can be worth noticing where it has taught you something exact, the way one shoe for both feet taught her.

cross_checks.claim: Handler had breast cancer and a mastectomy in 1970.
In 1976 she formed a company to make and market the Nearly Me prosthesis.
Nearly Me was made of liquid silicone with a polyurethane cover and foam back, in many sizes and separate left and right versions.
She fitted customers herself and used fitters, and fitted Betty Ford.
Sales passed $1 million by 1980, and she sold the company in 1991.

research_notes: Partner: Wikipedia and many derived pages name him Peyton Massey; Harvard's Schlesinger Library guide names Gerald Peyton; History.com says only that she worked with a prosthetics specialist. The story does not name him. Sales: the 2002 Los Angeles Times obituary says sales had passed $1 million by 1980; History.com says Ruthton reported sales in the millions by 1980; the story uses the conservative LA Times figure. The 1977 New York Times article, cited by History.com as about a million-dollar business, could not be opened (nytimes.com blocks automated requests), so the shoemaker quotation is taken from History.com's quotation of it. Buyer in 1991: History.com and Women in World History say Kimberly-Clark (a division of it); a retailer page says the brand went to Anita International in 1992 (possibly a later resale); the story says only that she sold the company in 1991. Founding year: 1976 per Schlesinger and TODAY; the LA Times obituary says only that she founded Ruthton after being forced out of Mattel. The company field gives both names because the product and later firm were called Nearly Me while the company she formed was Ruthton. Funding is set to unknown: no source says how the company was financed. The Mattel indictment is stated as the court record puts it (no-contest plea, fine and community service). History.com's 'I was supposed to whisper' quotation is ambiguous in context (Mattel investigation or cancer), so it is not used. The Smithsonian's Nearly Me objects and the Jewish Women's Archive entry block automated requests. Seneca's passage is about concealing poverty; it is applied by analogy.
